title: Isaac means laughter (Genesis 21:1–7)
hookLine: God has made me laugh, says Sarah at ninety

cards: There's a kind of laugh you can't help.
The one that bursts out when the impossible thing actually happens: the test comes back clear, the acceptance letter after years of no, the friend you thought you'd lost, standing at the door.
In Genesis, laughter keeps turning up around one promise. Abraham laughed when God first said Sarah would have a son; he fell on his face and laughed, the text says, at ninety-nine.
Sarah, listening at the tent door, laughed to herself. Both laughed because it was too much to believe. Today, they find out how it ends.

teach.b: Chapter twenty-one opens almost quietly, in the King James Bible: "And the LORD visited Sarah as he had said." As he had said. Twenty-five years after the call to go, the promise lands.
Sarah, around ninety, has a son, and Abraham, a hundred, names him Isaac, just as he'd been told. And the name is the joke, and the joy.
In Hebrew, Isaac is Yitzchak, which means he laughs. Every time anyone says this boy's name for the rest of his life, they'll be saying laughter.

teach.h: ALL THAT HEAR WILL LAUGH WITH ME.
teach.b: Then Sarah speaks: "God hath made me to laugh, so that all that hear will laugh with me." Think about how far she's come.
At the tent door at Mamre, her laugh was a disbelieving one, quiet, to herself, and then denied out of fear. Now it's out loud, and it's for everyone. All that hear will laugh with me.
She goes on: who would have said to Abraham that Sarah would nurse children? I've borne him a son in his old age.

teach.h: A LAUGH OF DOUBT, TURNED TO JOY.
teach.b: The same word, laugh, carries both meanings in this story: the laugh of doubt, and the laugh of joy. The text doesn't erase the first one. It turns it around.
Christians have often seen in Isaac's birth a picture of God doing what people think is impossible, and the letter to the Hebrews praises Sarah's faith in it. But the scene itself isn't a sermon.

teach.h: GOD HATH MADE ME TO LAUGH.
teach.b: It's an old woman holding a baby, laughing, and inviting everyone to laugh with her.

how: Many Christians speak of Sarah and Abraham as models of faith in God's promises, following the letter to the Hebrews, which praises Sarah for judging God faithful to his promise.

o: he hears: the name Hagar's son was given
the promised one: a title for Abraham's heir
he laughs: the name of Sarah's promised son

games.q: who laughed, and how — tap the pairs.
p: laughed to herself, then denied it

s: only Sarah laughed at the promise of a son
Abraham laughed first, falling on his face, in chapter seventeen.
Sarah's laugh at the birth is a quiet one, to herself
"all that hear will laugh with me."

games.q: you're Sarah, about ninety, holding the son you laughed about at the tent door. what do you say?
o: "God hath made me to laugh, so that all that hear will laugh with me."
games.why: the laugh of doubt becomes a laugh of joy, out loud, and for everyone.

practice: Think of a moment when something you'd given up on actually happened, or the funniest thing that happened this month, and let yourself smile at it. If a laugh comes, let it out, even alone, and notice how it feels in your body.
If you pray, you can give thanks for the joke and the joy.

wordCard.voice: Yitzchak. Hebrew for he laughs, the name given to Sarah's promised son, born after years of laughing in disbelief.

carryVoice: Your line: god made me laugh. Joy this big is meant to be shared. Day three hundred fifty-five.
